lessons.title: Ratio Reasoning: Convert Measurements within the Same System
lessons.objective: I can use ratio reasoning to convert between units within the same measurement system.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain a conversion using the words unit ratio, convert, measurement system, and per.

concept.heading: Converting inside one measurement system
concept.intro: Two measurements can only be compared when they are written in the same unit. Converting uses a special ratio — a unit ratio — that says how much of the smaller unit fits into exactly 1 of the larger unit.
concept.keyIdea: Converting Measurements (Same System). Formula: Quantity × (Unit Conversion Ratio) = New Quantity. 1. Identify the conversion factor (e.g. 1 ft = 12 in, 1 km = 1,000 m). 2. Larger to smaller unit: Multiply by the conversion factor. 3. Smaller to larger unit: Divide by the conversion factor

worked.title: Watch me check the ride height rule
lines: A ride requires riders to be at or above 44 inches tall. A child is 4 feet tall. The two measurements use different units, so I cannot compare them yet.

Both units belong to the customary system, and there are 12 inches in one foot. That relationship is the conversion factor. As a ratio it is 12 : 1 — a unit ratio, because it compares an amount to exactly 1 foot.
Inches are smaller than feet, so there will be MORE of them: I multiply. 4 × 12 = 48.
The child is 48 inches tall. Now the comparison is fair: 48 inches is greater than 44 inches, so the child can go on the ride.
linesEs: Un juego mecánico exige que quienes suban midan 44 pulgadas o más. Un niño mide 4 pies. Las dos medidas usan unidades distintas, así que todavía no puedo compararlas.

Las dos unidades pertenecen al sistema usual, y hay 12 pulgadas en un pie. Esa relación es el factor de conversión. Como razón es 12 : 1 — una razón unitaria, porque compara una cantidad con exactamente 1 pie.
Las pulgadas son más pequeñas que los pies, así que habrá más: multiplico. 4 × 12 = 48.
El niño mide 48 pulgadas. Ahora la comparación es justa: 48 pulgadas es más que 44 pulgadas, así que el niño sí puede subir al juego.
worked.titleEs: Mírame revisar la regla de estatura del juego

together.title: Let's do one together
lines: Diamond wants to drink 4 liters of water. Her bottle is marked in milliliters.
The conversion factor is 1,000 mL : 1 L. On a double number line, every 1 liter above matches 1,000 milliliters below.
Milliliters are smaller, so multiply: 4 × 1,000 = 4,000. So 4 liters = 4,000 milliliters.
Her bottle holds 500 milliliters. How many fills? Solve ? × 500 = 4,000. Since 8 × 500 = 4,000, she fills the bottle 8 times.
linesEs: Diamond quiere tomar 4 litros de agua. Su botella está marcada en mililitros.
El factor de conversión es 1,000 mL : 1 L. En una recta numérica doble, cada 1 litro de arriba corresponde a 1,000 mililitros abajo.
Los mililitros son más pequeños, así que multiplica: 4 × 1,000 = 4,000. Entonces 4 litros = 4,000 mililitros.
Su botella tiene capacidad de 500 mililitros. ¿Cuántas veces la llena? Resuelve ? × 500 = 4,000. Como 8 × 500 = 4,000, llena la botella 8 veces.

vocabulary.term: Convert Measurements within the Same System
vocabulary.definition: Rewriting a measurement in a different unit of the SAME system, such as feet into inches or liters into milliliters.
The ratio that links two units in the same measurement system, such as 12 inches to 1 foot. Within one system it is exact.
A ratio that compares an amount to exactly 1 unit of another quantity, like 12 inches to 1 foot.
vocabulary.example: 12 : 1 — twelve inches for every one foot

vocabulary.definition: To change a measurement from one unit to another without changing how much it is.
vocabulary.example: 4 ft and 48 in are the same height, written two ways

vocabulary.definition: A family of units that go together — customary units like inches and feet, or metric units like milliliters and liters.
vocabulary.example: Customary: 12 in = 1 ft · Metric: 1,000 mL = 1 L

vocabulary.definition: Two number lines lined up so matching tick marks show two units for the same amount.
A table of equal ratios that lets you scale a conversion up or down one row at a time.
vocabulary.example: 1 ft : 12 in, 2 ft : 24 in, 4 ft : 48 in

vocabulary.definition: The U.S. system of units: inch, foot, yard, mile, ounce, pound, cup, quart, gallon.
The base-10 system of units: meter, gram, liter.

lessons.title: Ratio Reasoning: Convert Measurements Between Systems
lessons.objective: I can use ratio reasoning to convert measurements between the customary and metric systems.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain a conversion between systems using the words conversion factor, approximately, customary, and metric.

concept.heading: Comparing across two measurement systems
concept.intro: Kilometers and miles both measure distance, but they come from different measurement systems, so the numbers cannot be compared directly. A conversion factor links the two systems, and a ratio table scales it up to the amount you need.
concept.keyIdea: Converting Measurements Between Systems. 1. Identify the conversion ratio connecting systems (e.g. 1 in = 2.54 cm, 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lbs). 2. Set up a ratio table or proportion aligning customary and metric units. 3. Multiply or divide by the conversion factor to compute the equivalent measurement

worked.title: Watch me compare two speed limits
lines: Evelyn sees a Canadian highway sign reading 100 kilometers per hour and wonders whether that is faster or slower than 100 miles per hour.
Kilometers are metric and miles are customary, so 100 and 100 cannot be compared as they stand. Both measure distance, so a conversion factor links them: 1 kilometer ≈ 0.6 mile, or the ratio 1 : 0.6.
I build a ratio table from that unit ratio. Kilometers 1, 10, 100 pair with miles 0.6, 6, 60 — each column multiplies both numbers by the same factor.
So 100 kilometers ≈ 60 miles, which means 100 kilometers per hour ≈ 60 miles per hour.
Now the comparison is fair: 100 miles per hour is faster, because in one hour you would travel 100 miles instead of only about 60.
linesEs: Evelyn ve un letrero de una carretera canadiense que dice 100 kilómetros por hora y se pregunta si eso es más rápido o más lento que 100 millas por hora.

Los kilómetros son métricos y las millas son del sistema usual, así que 100 y 100 no se pueden comparar tal como están. Las dos miden distancia, así que un factor de conversión las une: 1 kilómetro ≈ 0.6 milla, o la razón 1 : 0.6.
Armo una tabla de razones con esa razón unitaria. Los kilómetros 1, 10, 100 se emparejan con las millas 0.6, 6, 60 — cada columna multiplica los dos números por el mismo factor.
Entonces 100 kilómetros ≈ 60 millas, lo que significa que 100 kilómetros por hora ≈ 60 millas por hora.
Ahora la comparación es justa: 100 millas por hora es más rápido, porque en una hora recorrerías 100 millas en lugar de solo unas 60.
worked.titleEs: Mírame comparar dos límites de velocidad

together.title: Let's do one together
lines: Terrance needs flea medicine for a dog weighing 31 pounds, but the packages are labeled in kilograms.
The conversion factor is 1 pound ≈ 0.45 kilogram, so the ratio is 1 : 0.45.
Scale it with a ratio table: 10 lb ≈ 4.5 kg, 20 lb ≈ 9 kg, 30 lb ≈ 13.5 kg, 40 lb ≈ 18 kg.
31 pounds is just past 30, so the dog is a little more than 13.5 kilograms. That falls inside the package for dogs between 10 and 25 kilograms.
linesEs: Terrance necesita medicina contra pulgas para un perro que pesa 31 libras, pero los paquetes están etiquetados en kilogramos.
El factor de conversión es 1 libra ≈ 0.45 kilogramo, así que la razón es 1 : 0.45.
Escálala con una tabla de razones: 10 lb ≈ 4.5 kg, 20 lb ≈ 9 kg, 30 lb ≈ 13.5 kg, 40 lb ≈ 18 kg.
31 libras está apenas pasando las 30, así que el perro pesa un poco más de 13.5 kilogramos. Eso cae dentro del paquete para perros de entre 10 y 25 kilogramos.

vocabulary.definition: Rewriting a customary measurement as a metric one, or the reverse, so two amounts can be compared.
The ratio that links a unit in one system to a unit in the other, such as 1 mile to about 1.609 kilometers.
The measurement system used in the United States: inches, feet, miles, ounces, pounds, cups, quarts, gallons.
vocabulary.example: in · ft · mi · oz · lb · qt · gal

vocabulary.definition: The measurement system used in most of the world, built on tens: centimeters, meters, kilometers, grams, kilograms, liters.
vocabulary.example: cm · m · km · g · kg · mL · L

vocabulary.definition: Close to, but not exactly equal. A rounded conversion factor gives an approximate result, written with ≈; an exact conversion uses =.
A table of equal ratios used to scale a conversion factor up to the amount you actually need.
Checking that the size of an answer makes sense for the situation.
vocabulary.example: A bigger unit should give a smaller number.

vocabulary.definition: A problem that needs two or more operations done in order.

Compare that conversion with 1 foot = 12 inches. Name the starting and ending units every time.

support.prompt: There are 12 inches in 1 foot. How many inches are in 5 feet?
support.explanation: Inches are smaller than feet, so multiply by the unit ratio: 5 × 12 = 60 inches.
feedback: That subtracts 12 − 5. Converting is not a subtraction.
That adds 5 + 12. Converting scales the amount, so multiply.
hints: Write the unit ratio first: 12 inches : 1 foot.
Inches are smaller, so the number gets bigger — multiply.

support.prompt: There are 1,000 milliliters in 1 liter. How many milliliters are in 3 liters?
support.explanation: Multiply by the unit ratio: 3 × 1,000 = 3,000 milliliters.
feedback: 30 is far too small — one liter alone is already 1,000 mL.
That adds instead of multiplying.
hints: The unit ratio is 1,000 mL : 1 L.
Milliliters are smaller, so multiply.

support.prompt: There are 16 ounces in 1 pound. How many pounds is 48 ounces?
support.explanation: Pounds are the LARGER unit, so divide: 48 ÷ 16 = 3 pounds.
feedback: That subtracts 48 − 16.
That adds 48 + 16. Converting to a larger unit divides.
That multiplies. Multiplying goes to the smaller unit, not the larger one.
hints: Which unit is larger, an ounce or a pound?
Converting to the larger unit takes fewer of them, so divide.

support.prompt: A child is 4 feet tall. A ride requires 44 inches. Can the child ride?
choices: Yes, because 4 feet = 48 inches, which is more than 44
You cannot compare feet and inches
support.explanation: Convert first so both measurements use the same unit: 4 × 12 = 48 inches. 48 > 44, so the child can ride.
feedback: 4 feet and 44 inches use different units — comparing the bare numbers is what the conversion prevents.
You can compare them, once both are written in the same unit.
hints: You cannot compare two different units directly.
Convert the feet to inches with the 12 : 1 unit ratio.
Then compare 48 with 44.

steps: Step 1: There are 12 inches in 1 foot.
Step 3: So 5 feet is about 0.42 inches.
support.explanation: Step 2 divides when it should multiply. Inches are SMALLER than feet, so it takes more of them: 5 × 12 = 60 inches.
hints: Is an inch bigger or smaller than a foot?
If the unit is smaller, does the number get bigger or smaller?

support.prompt: 1 kilometer ≈ 0.6 mile. About how many miles is 5 kilometers?
support.explanation: Scale the conversion factor by 5: 0.6 × 5 = 3 miles.
feedback: That adds 5 + 0.6 instead of scaling the ratio.
A kilometer is shorter than a mile, so the number of miles must be smaller than 5.
hints: Write the conversion factor as a ratio: 1 : 0.6.
Multiply both parts by 5.

support.prompt: 1 pound ≈ 0.45 kilogram. About how many kilograms is 10 pounds?
feedback: That adds instead of scaling.
That converts the wrong direction — a kilogram is heavier than a pound.
hints: The ratio is 1 lb : 0.45 kg.
Multiply both parts by 10.

support.prompt: Which pair of units comes from two DIFFERENT measurement systems?
support.explanation: Miles are customary and kilometers are metric, so comparing them requires a between-systems conversion. The other pairs stay inside one system.
feedback: Both inches and feet are customary.
Both cups and quarts are customary.
Both grams and kilograms are metric.
hints: Sort each unit as customary or metric.
Metric units include meter, gram, liter and their prefixes.
Which pair has one of each?

support.prompt: A sign in Mexico gives a distance of 80 kilometers. Using 1 km ≈ 0.6 mi, about how far is that in miles?
support.explanation: 0.6 × 80 = 48 miles. Because a kilometer is shorter than a mile, the number of miles is smaller than the number of kilometers.
feedback: The number must change, because the units are different sizes.
That divides instead of multiplying, converting the wrong direction.
hints: Scale the ratio 1 : 0.6 up to 80 kilometers.
Multiply 0.6 by 80.
Should the miles number be bigger or smaller than 80?

steps: Setup: 1 kilometer ≈ 0.6 mile. About how many miles is 20 kilometers?
support.explanation: Step 2 divides when the ratio should be scaled up by multiplying: 0.6 × 20 = 12 miles.
hints: Is a kilometer longer or shorter than a mile?
Should the answer in miles be more or less than 20?

support.prompt: Predict the converted length for these settings. Give the answer in centimeters. Round to four decimal places if needed.
support.explanation: 5 × 2.54 = 12.7. 1 inch = exactly 2.54 centimeters. Divide centimeters by 2.54 to convert back.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.

core.prompt: Diamond needs 4 liters of water. Her bottle holds 500 milliliters. How many times must she fill it?
core.explanation: Convert first: 4 L = 4,000 mL. Then solve ? × 500 = 4,000, giving 8 fills.
feedback: 2 × 500 = 1,000 mL, only one liter.
4 is the number of liters, not the number of fills.
40 × 500 = 20,000 mL, which is 20 liters.
hints: Get both amounts into the same unit first.
4 liters is 4,000 milliliters.
What times 500 equals 4,000?

steps: Setup: A recipe needs 2 pounds of flour. The scale reads in ounces (16 oz = 1 lb).
Step 1: The unit ratio is 16 ounces : 1 pound.
Step 3: The scale reads 40 ounces, so there is not enough flour.
core.explanation: Step 3 compares correctly but concludes backwards. The recipe needs 32 ounces and the scale shows 40 ounces. Since 40 > 32, there is MORE than enough flour — 8 ounces extra.
hints: Steps 1 and 2 are correct — check the comparison.
Which is larger, 40 ounces or 32 ounces?
Does more on the scale mean not enough?

core.prompt: A dog weighs 31 pounds. Flea medicine comes in packages for 4–10 kg, 10–25 kg, and 25–40 kg. Which package is correct?
core.explanation: 31 pounds ≈ 0.45 × 31 ≈ 14 kilograms, which falls inside the 10–25 kilogram package.
feedback: 4–10 kg would be about 9–22 pounds, lighter than this dog.
25–40 kg would be about 55–88 pounds, far heavier than this dog.
The ranges are in kilograms — convert the 31 pounds first, and it fits.
hints: The packages are in kilograms but the dog is weighed in pounds.
Convert 31 pounds using 1 lb ≈ 0.45 kg.
About 14 kilograms — which range holds it?

steps: Setup: A recipe calls for 2 pounds of flour. The scale is metric. (1 lb ≈ 0.45 kg)
core.explanation: Step 3 claims an exact equality. The conversion factor 0.45 is rounded (1 pound is about 0.4536 kilogram), so the result must be written 2 pounds ≈ 0.9 kilogram.
hints: The arithmetic in Step 2 is correct.
Look closely at the symbol used in Step 3.
Is 1 pound exactly 0.45 kilogram?

steps: Setup: Convert 4 liters to milliliters, then find how many 250-mL cups it fills.
stretch.explanation: Step 2 multiplies when it should divide. The question asks how many 250-mL cups fit inside 4,000 mL, which is a division: 4,000 ÷ 250 = 16 cups.
hints: Step 1 is correct. Look at what Step 2 asks for.
How many groups of 250 fit into 4,000?

stretch.prompt: Michael's mother is setting four fence posts. Each post needs 250 ounces of concrete mix, one bag holds 80 ounces, and each bag needs 1 quart of water. How many bags and how many cups of water does she need? Show your conversions.
stretch.explanation: Total mix: 4 posts × 250 ounces = 1,000 ounces. Bags needed: 1,000 ÷ 80 = 12.5, and you cannot buy half a bag, so she needs 13 bags. Water: each bag takes 1 quart, so 13 bags take 13 quarts. Converting to cups with the unit ratio 4 cups : 1 quart, 13 × 4 = 52 cups of water. The two conversions go opposite ways: ounces to bags divides (a bag is the larger unit), while quarts to cups multiplies (a cup is the smaller unit).
hints: Find the total ounces of mix first.
Divide by the ounces in one bag — then think about whether you can buy part of a bag.
Convert quarts to cups with the 4 : 1 unit ratio.

steps: Setup: Which is longer, 5 kilometers or 5 miles? (1 km ≈ 0.6 mi)
Step 2: The units are different, so I compare the numbers: they are equal.
Step 3: 5 kilometers is the same distance as 5 miles.
stretch.explanation: Step 2 compares numbers that are measured in different units. Convert first: 5 kilometers ≈ 0.6 × 5 = 3 miles. Comparing 3 miles with 5 miles shows that 5 miles is the longer distance.
hints: What is different about the two measurements besides the number?
Convert one of them so both use the same unit.

stretch.prompt: The Golden Gate Bridge can hold about 35,924,000 pounds. An average midsize car weighs about 1,524 kilograms. Using 1 kilogram ≈ 2.2 pounds, about how many midsize cars could be on the bridge at one time? Explain each step, and say why your answer is an estimate.
stretch.explanation: First convert one car's mass into pounds so both amounts share a unit: 1,524 × 2.2 ≈ 3,353 pounds per car. Then divide the bridge's capacity by the weight of one car: 35,924,000 ÷ 3,353 ≈ 10,700 cars. The answer is an estimate for two reasons: the conversion factor 2.2 is rounded (1 kilogram is about 2.2046 pounds), and 1,524 kilograms is itself an average car mass, not an exact one. Reporting 'about 10,700 cars' is honest; reporting 10,714.6 cars would claim precision the inputs never had.
hints: The two amounts are in different systems — convert one of them first.
Convert the car's mass to pounds with 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb.
Then divide the bridge capacity by the weight of one car.
